speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: The Enlistment Act entrenched National Service (NS), first introduced in 1967.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Both the Enlistment Act and the Requisition of Resources Act have served Singapore well over the past five decades to build up our security forces to protect Singapore's sovereignty and to maintain law and order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: The main provisions of the Enlistment Act and the Requisition of Resources Act continue to be relevant and need no amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: However, there is a need to amend the Acts to keep pace with a modernised, digitalised Singapore that is quite different from the Singapore 50 years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Hence, the amendments proposed formalise present practices as well as remove obsolete clauses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: I will now go through the amendments in detail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: First, on the amendments to keep up with developments in digital technology, section 30 of the Enlistment Act – Orders and Notices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: First, the proposed amendments to section 30 of the Enlistment Act concerning orders and notices that are issued under the Enlistment Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Under section 30 of the current Enlistment Act, orders and notices to NS or SAF personnel are served through various means, such as through telephone calls, radio or television broadcast and registered post.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Over the past two decades, notices and orders have also been served through electronic means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: An Operationally Ready National Serviceman, or NSman for short, is now informed of his NS call-up activity via an SMS and in his NS Portal account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: He can acknowledge the notice either by replying to the SMS directly, or by logging on to the NS Portal to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Should he fail to acknowledge the call-up notice which is sent to him electronically, he will receive another SMS reminder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: And if he still fails to respond to that reminder, he is sent a hardcopy version of the notice via registered post.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: As the practice of receiving notices and orders by electronic means is now well accepted and entrenched, the proposed amendments to section 30 will formalise this into the amended Enlistment Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: As with the existing modes of service, such as telephone calls, radio or television broadcast and registered post, these electronic means of service come with the same deeming provisions, which presume Enlistment Act notices and orders are received and read within a fixed timeframe after delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Deeming provisions ensure that a recipient cannot feign ignorance of his NS obligations when notices and orders have been duly served.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Members may worry that recipients may receive many digital notifications, such as emails or SMSes, in the course of a normal day and could genuinely miss out on reading some of these electronic notifications from the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF), SAF or the Home Team.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: First, we will continue today's practice of issuing orders and notices to individuals through various channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Specifically, should individuals fail to respond to orders or notices issued by electronic means, MINDEF will follow on to serve them with notices or orders using existing modes of service, such as telephone calls or registered post.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: This ensures that we make every attempt and make every effort to have the orders and notices reach their intended recipient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Second, MINDEF will also codify in subsidiary legislation the steps which we will take in serving orders and notices on individuals such that people will have the full assurance that their attention will be adequately brought to the obligations they need to fulfil for NS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Those who provide such consent can withdraw that consent at any time, should they choose to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Next, I will move on to speak about section 41 of the Requisition of Resources Act under the section of orders, notices and requisitions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Similar changes regarding the electronic delivery of orders, notices and requisitions will be made to section 41 of the Requisition of Resources Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: In the same way, NSmen are notified of their call-ups today, civil resource owners are currently also notified of the requisition of their resources via an SMS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Another SMS will be sent if there is no acknowledgement of the first SMS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: If these two SMSes – the first one and the reminder – elicit no response, MINDEF will contact the civil resource owners via existing means of service, such as by telephone call or personal delivery of the hardcopy notice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: This requisition system has been used during exercises and civil resource owners have responded well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Our amendments to section 41 of the Requisition of Resources Act will, therefore, similarly legislate the inclusion of electronic means of service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Similar to the Enlistment Act, safeguards will also be in place to ensure that we have made every effort and every attempt to reach the civil resource owners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: In this vein, the deeming provisions for electronic means of service are only meant to be applied onto the few civil resource owners who fail to comply with their obligations and remain uncontactable despite multiple attempts to reach them through the whole variety of channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Consent will also be sought from the civil resource owners before orders and notices sent by electronic means can be presumed and deemed to have been received and read by them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Those who provide such consent can also withdraw their consent at any time, should they choose to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Today, pre-enlistees from age 13 years and full-time National Servicemen (or NSFs) are required to possess a valid Exit Permit for any travel overseas that goes beyond three months' duration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: For NSmen, the requirement is more relaxed in recognition of their higher likelihood of staying or working overseas for longer durations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: NSmen will need to possess a valid Exit Permit for any travel overseas that exceeds a year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: We will make the relevant consequential amendments to section 52 of the Immigration Act, which empowers an immigration officer to act to prevent an NS-liable person from leaving Singapore, if that immigration officer has reason to believe that the individual does not possess an Exit Permit as required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: This is to enable the immigration officer to inquire into this suspicion and require the person to produce for inspection the valid Exit Permit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: Next, I will touch on section 27 of the Enlistment Act which deals with unaccountable periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: The proposed amendment at section 27(2) of the Enlistment Act specifies the types of periods that do not count towards the fulfilment of an NSman's NS liability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: We will remove and update references within the Enlistment Act and Requisition of Resources Act that are now obsolete.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: For example, references to "telex" as a mode of service of orders or notices will be removed because we no longer use this means to send out notices and orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: We will also add references to the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) where necessary, to account for the fact that our NSmen are also deployed to the SPF and SCDF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: We will also update references in the offence provisions of the Requisition of Resources Act to align with other national legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: These amendments are administrative updates that do not impact existing NS or civil resource requisition policies or obligations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How) (for the Minister for Defence)
text: These amendments allow us to modernise and tidy up both the Enlistment Act and the Requisition of Resources Act.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: National Service (NS) plays a critical role in reinforcing the Total Defence concept.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Total Defence encourages the active involvement of all citizens in safeguarding the security and well-being of our nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Enlistment into NS is a crucial aspect of the military component of Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Since the National Service (Amendment) Bill was passed in March 1967, more than a million male Singaporeans and permanent residents have served NS.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Enlistees can serve in the military, Police and the Singapore Civil Defence Force.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Conscription is an essential component of national security, providing rapid and robust responses to external and internal threats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: NS also contributes to the creation of a national identity that cuts across ethnic races, social classes and religions, as well as bolstering social resilience against instabilities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: I support the Bill and I would like to seek clarifications on the following.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: The amendments in section 30 on orders, notices, permits and appointments are necessary as communications today are predominantly digitalised via short message service (SMS), emails and electronic service platforms.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: What safeguards are in place to address concerns related to the acknowledgment or consent requirement for electronic service?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: How will individuals be informed and given the option to consent?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: How would the Ministry prevent or minimise the impact of potential digital attacks and fraudulent communications by criminals and hostile agents to undermine our defence forces?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Pertaining section 52 of the Immigration Act, how do the immigration officers determine if a person subject to the Enlistment Act has the required exit permit?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the timely amendments in section 24, which explicitly allows persons who perform the listed services to claim reimbursement for remuneration derived from self-employment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: I hope MINDEF and MHA can arrange for consultative sessions with the insurance practitioners, financial planners, property advisers, private hire drivers and platform workers to have a deeper understanding of their remuneration structures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we have no quarrel with the updates proposed in the Bill, we note that the Bill does not make any amendments to the statutory length of liability to render full-time NS, as provided in section 12 of the Enlistment Act 1970.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since Independence, our SAF, SPF and SCDF have become world-class institutions, and this success has come on the backs of generations of full-time NSmen (NSFs) who have given two or two-and-a-half years of their lives to serve the nation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This sacrifice in youth comes at significant cost to the individual.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, the duration of full-time NS must be carefully calibrated and reviewed from time to time, based on our nation's defence needs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the time, Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean, who was then Minister for Defence, explained in a Ministerial Statement that this was possible because of the SAF's technological transformation to the Third Generation SAF and a 15% and 20% increase in the annual intake of NSFs over 10 years starting in 2006.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister Teo also told the House that MINDEF had concluded that the two years of NS duration will be able to be sustained over the long term even after this 10-year surge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Minister several questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, are the considerations and conclusions made by Senior Minister Teo in June 2004 still valid?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, by retaining this provision in the Enlistment Act, does this mean the Government expects that the duration of full-time NS may be reverted to two-and-a-half years at some point in the future?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP calls on the Government to continue reviewing the duration of full-time NS based on operational needs, demographic changes and technological advancements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where possible, without compromising on operational readiness, training standards and the ability of our uniformed services to achieve their mission, we would support further reductions in our dependence on large numbers of NSFs and further reductions in the duration of full-time National Service.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a timely amendment of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is to reflect the modern landscape of national service and voluntary service.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I have several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, on liability, ranks and the removal of part-time NS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to understand how these extensions align with the overall manpower needs of both agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This clarity is critical in ensuring effective and efficient operations and public service within the SPF and SCDF.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, on the deletion of section 14(1)(b)(ii) relating to part-time NS, we require a clear understanding of the rationale behind this decision and its potential consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this decision align with the current defence strategies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure the continued effectiveness of our NS framework?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, on the use of technology for the service of notices and orders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments to section 30 allowing for the service of notices and orders through modern technological avenues like SMS, email and dedicated platforms are commendable steps towards modernisation and streamlined communications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I seek further clarification on several aspects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, how are these changes aligned with emerging advancements in technology to improve efficiency in communication, specifically in the context of NS and enlistment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given rapid technological advancements, is the Bill sufficiently flexible to accommodate future innovations in communication technology?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, while embracing technology's benefits, we must remain mindful of potential challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Concerns regarding fake notices, potential misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) for manipulation and potential for abuse of these systems deserve careful consideration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to ensure that robust safeguards and clear guidelines are in place to prevent such issues and maintain the integrity of the communication process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, as a committed SAF volunteer myself, I take a keen interest in the proposed enhancements to volunteer protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note the revisions set out in clause 13 of the Bill regarding references to volunteer service within the SAF's People's Defence Force and the Police Force Act's Special Constabulary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State explain how these changes translate into concrete safeguards for all SAF volunteers under the relevant sections of the Enlistment Act?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, how does this impact the SPF's Volunteer Special Constabulary programme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, can the Ministry provide elaboration on how these amendments ensure the welfare and rights of our diverse volunteer community?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By ensuring all volunteers feel protected, valued and supported, we can continue to attract and retain dedicated individuals who bolster our nation's strength.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, I seek clarification regarding the Minister's broader powers to make regulations under the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Flexibility is indeed critical in adapting to a changing environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is equally important to ensure that such power is not wielded in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While increased flexibility must be justified in certain scenarios, we must ensure sufficient clarity and transparency in these regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear regulatory frameworks are the bedrock of effective implementation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the nature of warfare is no longer defined by clashing armies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recent self-radicalisation cases are also stark reminders that we must remain vigilant in ensuring security within our borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must remember that national security is not solely the responsibility of the military.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We commemorated Total Defence Day yesterday and are reminded that this is a shared endeavour, requiring the collective commitment of every citizen.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have highlighted several clarifications in my speech, namely: First, aligning manpower needs with the extensions of specific ranks in SPF and SCDF.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also need to understand the rationale behind removing part-time NS and its consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, having safeguards with technological advancements – mitigate potential risks like fake notices, AI misuse and abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure robust communication practices and integrity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, enhancing volunteer protection – translate proposed changes into concrete safeguards for all SAF volunteers, ensuring their welfare, rights and continued contribution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And lastly, having greater transparency in ministerial regulations – balance flexibility with clear frameworks, robust Parliamentary oversight and public scrutiny for effective implementation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By addressing these concerns, and ensuring clarity and transparency, we can strengthen the Enlistment Act and build a future-proof NS framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most of the amendments are done to update the Bill and to take into account developments in technology and it is naturally sensible to include these developments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It says these modes of service may only be used with the enlistee's express consent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the set-up of the section is sensible and, in principle, if an enlistee agrees to accept service by any of these methods, it would be efficient for both MINDEF and the enlistee to communicate in this way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: MINDEF's current practice, as confirmed by Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How, already involves the use of these methods, except that if there is no express acknowledgement of receipt by the NSman, MINDEF then follows up with the conventional notice by registered post.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is because under the current legislation, MINDEF cannot assume notice has been received simply by sending an email or SMS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think there is some benefit with MINDEF's current method of sending a follow-up in the event the enlistee does not acknowledge an SMS or email and my concern is that with the change in legislation, MINDEF may stop doing this because it can simply assume that enlistees have received notice of the call-up from the deemed notice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In general, while an enlistee may give consent to receiving notice by SMS or email, sometimes, life events catch up and the SMS numbers or email addresses may change.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is especially so if the person gives his consent, say, at the end of NS, but then goes on to study or work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I acknowledge that it is an individual's responsibility to update MINDEF on his latest contact details and to check these, but any penalty for not updating contact details should not be at the severity of getting charged for failing to attend the call-up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, there are increasingly sophisticated spam filters in many email accounts that may block system-generated emails like call-up notices.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, even if the details are up to date, the notices may get accidentally filtered out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is good and, in my view, important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It means that notwithstanding the change in legislation, the useful practice will continue.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: They recognise the importance of keeping our NS and civil resources requisition systems effective and up-to-date.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: First, on amendments to section 30 of the Enlistment Act on orders and notices, which is on the acknowledgement and consent safeguards.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: On orders and notices issued as referenced at section 30 of the Enlistment Act, and in reply to Mr Don Wee and Mr Vikram Nair, I state once again very clearly that every effort will be made to ensure that orders and notices issued through electronic means reach their intended recipient.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Furthermore, I want to again emphasise that should recipients fail to respond to these electronic orders and notices, then we will use other existing modes of service, such as through telephone calls as well as registered post in order to mail them the hard copy.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Indeed, the whole intent of these amendments is to modernise the Act so that it includes means of communication that is used by everybody every day.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It is just keeping up with the times.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It is not the intention of this amendment to take away any sense of being properly informed in time.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: These percentages, we think, will go up and this just formalises the lived reality.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And as Mr Vikram Nair mentioned, that is the practice now and it will continue.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Those who provide such consent can withdraw their consent at any time should they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Individuals will be able to provide or withdraw such consent whenever they transact with MINDEF and SAF, such as through the NS Portal when they register for NS or when applying for an Exit Permit.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Individuals will also be given the option to withdraw their consent at any time via the NS Portal.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on securing electronic communications against digital attacks and fraud.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: With regard to security against digital attacks, scams and fraud, certainly, these efforts and improvements on the part of MINDEF and the SAF, and the Home Team, will be an ongoing affair and it will just keep improving over time as technology improves and as we come to know of different developments on the part of the criminal fraternity and how we can be one step ahead of them.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: This is an example where we also have to move with the times.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, it is not just by modernising the channels, but also by keeping in touch very much with how these channels are being used or indeed, being misused to harm and cheat people, and then, we can actually overcome that as time goes on.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It will be ceaseless effort and we are committed to doing that.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: We will also regularly conduct vulnerability assessments, penetration tests and audits on our IT systems, such as the NS Portal.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: These systems are also monitored 24/7 to quickly detect and neutralise any malicious activity.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Individuals can also call or email the NS Call Centre to verify the authenticity of any SMS, email or message that they received purporting to be from MINDEF, SAF or the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked if the changes to section 30 of the Enlistment Act are sufficiently flexible to accommodate future innovations in communications technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Should MINDEF begin utilising new technologies to issue orders or notices to individuals, then they would be covered in a newly proposed section 30(2)(n), or they can be prescribed by the Minister for Defence in subsidiary legislation under the new proposed section 30(2)(o).

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on amendments to section 32 of the Enlistment Act touching on Exit Permits.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the consequential amendment to section 52 of the Immigration Act and how immigration officers may determine if a person subject to the Enlistment Act has the required Exit Permit.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Actually, the immigration officer today, if he suspects anybody to not possess the right documents in order to enter or to exit Singapore, has already the powers to inquire.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, the amendment that we are proposing in this Bill is to make it clear because, just as we are making it clear who is liable for NS and to have an Exit Permit before leaving Singapore, we just want to make this consequential amendment in the Immigration Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: If an immigration officer has reason to believe that the person requires an Exit Permit, for example if the person is a male citizen or Permanent Resident of NS-liable age and indicates that he is going to be overseas for a long time – for example, he is going to be overseas for a year – then the immigration officer may request to sight, to look at the person's Exit Permit or a relevant written exemption, in order to allow him to leave Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It is not a new power, but this is just to make it very clear for all parties involved.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on the administrative amendments, is a clarification on liability to serve full-time NS which is section 12 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The amendments simply update the Enlistment Act to now include references to the SPF and SCDF, because NSFs are also sent over to the SPF and SCDF.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And for completeness in this revision exercise, we included the rank structures across the SPF and SCDF to correspond and commensurate with the equivalent in the SAF, for clarity again.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: I note Mr Leong Mun Wai also spoke about this provision for a maximum duration of NS.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: One of the things we often say about Singapore is that we have no natural resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And at the same time, precisely because all we have is our people, then how we use their time is important and there must be a good purpose for asking our people to contribute their time to do things under the law as a requirement.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The intent of that section to have been in the law in the first place is to define a maximum.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: By defining a maximum, what it does is this.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It actually put it onto the Government to make sure that whatever you are doing, in order to require citizens to give off their time to defend this country, you work within this maximum period of up to two-and-a-half years.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: It does not say that you must use two-and-a-half years.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The idea is very clear and by that very act of reducing it in 2004, the stance of the Government is also very clear, which is that we honour the sacrifice of our people in providing time to together defend this country.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And we will not want to take any more time from them than what is necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean at that time, the Defence Minister, had looked at the overall situation, the security situation, and determined that two years was appropriate.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also asked whether or not this continual review of requirements will be something quite standard in the way in which MINDEF would look at the requirements of manpower, the answer will be yes.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: We stand by this commitment to say that we thank our citizens for contributing their time to serve this country in NS.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: We commit to using their time the best way possible and not to require of them more than is necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And as part of this, we will constantly review requirements, processes, technologies, more productive methods.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, I move on to deletion of the Part-Time NS reference in section 14 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: As for deleting the reference to Part-Time NS at section 14(1)(b)(ii) of the Enlistment Act, actually there are no practical consequences because the clause is obsolete.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, we are just taking out something that is obsolete.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on self-employed NSmen and Make-Up Pay (MUP) under section 24 of the Enlistment Act, let me thank Mr Don Wee for his support for the amendment to section 24 of the Enlistment Act to explicitly allow for self-employed NSmen, just like employed NSmen, to claim remuneration for losses in their civilian income, or Make-Up Pay (MUP), when they attend Operationally Ready National Service (ORNS) activities.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Self-employed NSmen can also choose to submit supporting documents to appeal for a different MUP amount, because of their individual circumstances, if they believe that the amount automatically calculated for them is incorrect or not fair to them.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: They can submit their documents and then, each case will be carefully looked into.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on voluntary service in Part 6 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the amendments to Part 6 of the Enlistment Act, where references to voluntary service in the People's Defence Force of the SAF and the Special Constabulary of the SPF are being removed.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: There will be no change to the current statutory protections that are already accorded to these voluntary services under the respective Acts, such as the SAF Act, the Police Force Act and Civil Defence Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: For SAF volunteers, we are removing mention of the People's Defence Force because it is also obsolete.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, there is a duplication and, as a result, we are just taking out the duplication and having that deleted.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Once again, at this point, I just want to reiterate on behalf of MINDEF, SAF as well as the Home Team our heartfelt thanks to all our NS officers, NSFs, NSmen, through all these generations, our volunteers, for their selfless contributions, for their devotion to the defence of this country.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Their efforts are invaluable in continuing to build a strong SAF, SPF and SCDF so that, together, we can protect Singapore against threats and stand ready in all kinds of crisis scenarios.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Next, on the Minister's regulation-making powers under section 37 of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the amendments to section 37 of the Enlistment Act, as well as to clarify the Minister's powers to make regulations under the Enlistment Act and how we would guard against the potential misuse of such powers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: He says not to have the power to regulate in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Indeed, it will not be acting in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The amendment to section 37 of the Enlistment Act simply clarifies the language that any reference to the term "prescribe" in the Act means that it can be prescribed via the Regulations made by the Minister for Defence.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The Minister for Defence has the power to make the Regulations.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, this clarifies the language of what is the meaning of "prescribe".

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And even when amendments to Regulations are made, then they will also be published in the Government Gazette.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Therefore, it is fully transparent to the public.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: And where there are queries, again, this can be debated.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: The Enlistment Act and the Requisition of Resources Act have served Singapore well.
